summary: Defines two MIB modules for managing MAC bridges. One covers the traffic classes and enhanced multicast filtering of IEEE 802.1D, and the other covers VLANs as specified in IEEE 802.1Q. It supplements RFC 4188, obsoletes RFC 2674, and is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A dashboard for network switches: it lets a management program read and change settings such as traffic priorities and virtual groups.

subtitle: The SNMP management objects that let you configure a network switch's traffic priorities, multicast filtering and VLANs.

tldr.problem: Network bridges (layer 2 switches) gained traffic classes, multicast filtering and virtual LANs from IEEE 802.1D and 802.1Q, but a management station had no standard SNMP objects to configure or monitor them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two MIB modules: P-BRIDGE-MIB for traffic classes and multicast filtering, and Q-BRIDGE-MIB for VLANs. Both supplement the BRIDGE-MIB of RFC 4188.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 2674 as the standards-track definition of these objects, adds restricted group and VLAN registration controls, and defines three shared VLAN-ID textual conventions.

today: RFC 4363 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2674, and it supplements the BRIDGE-MIB of RFC 4188. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Managing Bridges with SNMP
sections.content:
A bridge connects LAN segments below the network layer. These devices are often known as 'layer 2 switches'. The transparent method of bridging is defined by IEEE 802.1D-1998, and its managed objects live in the BRIDGE-MIB (RFC 4188).

IEEE 802.1Q-2003 adds virtual bridged LANs: one physical bridged network supports several logical ones, each offering a service about the same as 802.1D. A VLAN can be seen as a group of end-stations on multiple LAN segments that communicate as if they were on a single LAN. IEEE 802.1Q defines port-based VLANs and port-and-protocol-based VLANs, and this memo defines the objects for managing port-based VLANs.

The memo is standards-track. It supplements RFC 4188 and obsoletes RFC 2674. Objects are defined with SMIv2 and accessed through SNMP, as in the Internet-Standard Management Framework (RFC 3410).
sections.plainLanguage: A switch is a box that passes messages between computers. This document says how a manager can ask the box questions and give it orders from far away.

sections.title: What Is Included and What Is Left Out
sections.content:
The modules try to match the manageable objects of IEEE 802.1D and 802.1Q, but a subjective judgement was made to omit the objects most costly to implement in an agent and least essential for fault and configuration management.

The RFC lists what was dropped. Examples include the 802.1Q operations to reset the bridge and reset the VLAN bridge, the filtering database size, and the notifications for group registration failure, VLAN registration failure and learning constraint violation, all marked 'not considered useful'. Some counts are not given as objects at all; instead you count rows in tables, such as the rows in dot1qStaticUnicastTable plus dot1qStaticMulticastTable for the number of static filtering entries.

For history, the original BRIDGE-MIB (RFC 1493) started from a small set of essential objects and limited the total number of objects, and this document keeps that spirit.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not add a dial for everything. They left out the dials that were hard to build and that nobody really needed.

sections.title: Two MIB Modules
sections.content:
P-BRIDGE-MIB (the extended bridge MIB) manages the traffic class and multicast filtering enhancements of IEEE 802.1D-1998, including Restricted Group Registration from IEEE 802.1t. It is organized into subtrees: dot1dExtBase (device-wide settings and capabilities, including per-device GARP and GMRP configuration), dot1dPriority (priority queuing, user_priority handling and mapping to traffic classes), dot1dGarp and dot1dGmrp. It also adds dot1dTpHCPortTable and dot1dTpPortOverflowTable, which extend the BRIDGE-MIB with statistics for high-capacity interfaces when 32-bit counters are inadequate.

Q-BRIDGE-MIB (the virtual bridge MIB) manages the VLAN enhancements of IEEE 802.1Q-2003, including Restricted VLAN Registration (802.1u) and VLAN Classification by Protocol and Port (802.1v). Its subtrees are dot1qBase (for all VLAN bridges), dot1qTp (the dynamic filtering databases), dot1qStatic (static filtering entries), dot1qVlan (VLAN configuration, per-port VLAN objects, statistics and learning constraints) and dot1vProtocol.

Some BRIDGE-MIB objects must be indexed differently in a VLAN environment, so the Q-BRIDGE-MIB effectively duplicates them with new indexing. A device that has no VLANs but does support extended filtering should use a fixed dot1qFdbId or dot1qVlanIndex; the value 1 is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two instruction manuals. One covers who goes first and who gets which messages. The other covers splitting one big network into separate private groups.

sections.title: Shared VLAN-ID Types
sections.content:
Several MIB documents had each defined their own way to write a VLAN-ID, which may lead to confusion and unnecessary complexity. The Q-BRIDGE-MIB therefore defines three new textual conventions, VlanIdOrAny, VlanIdOrNone and VlanIdOrAnyOrNone, which should be reused by other MIB modules.

A real VLAN-ID is 1 to 4094. The special value 4095 means any VLAN (a wildcard) and 0 means no VLAN. For example, an object could say which VLAN to accept packets of a given protocol on: a specific 802.1q tag, any tag, or no tag. Any object using these types should explain what 'any VLAN' or 'no VLAN' means in its own DESCRIPTION.

The Q-BRIDGE-MIB also defines VlanIndex for indexing per-VLAN tables, where values above 4095 stand for VLANs local to an agent, and PortList, a bit string in which each bit stands for one bridge port.

The IEEE confirmed that 0 and 4095 are not used for identifying a specific VLAN-ID, so they are safe to use this way (see the RFC's Appendix A).
sections.plainLanguage: A VLAN number is like a classroom number. This document adds two special answers: 'any classroom' and 'no classroom', so forms can say them clearly.

sections.title: Fitting In with Other MIBs
sections.content:
The bridge MIB modules do not stand alone. Full support needs sysDescr and sysUpTime from the SNMPv2-MIB (RFC 3418) and ifIndex, ifType, ifDescr, ifPhysAddress and ifLastChange from the IF-MIB (RFC 2863). Each bridge port is associated with one interface in ifTable, though in some cases several ports share one interface. Port numbers run from 1 to dot1dBaseNumPorts.

VLANs are not assumed to appear in ifTable. Higher-layer entities attached to a VLAN, such as IP interfaces, should be shown there as propVirtual(53), not protocol-specific types. The RFC also notes that ifStackTable cannot capture 802.1Q, which distinguishes ingress from egress VLAN bindings, so separate objects configure which ports belong to which VLANs.

For BRIDGE-MIB, the dot1dBase and dot1dStp subtrees are unchanged. With multiple filtering databases, dot1dStaticTable merges entries from all of them and should be read-only, with writes done through dot1qStaticUnicastTable and dot1qStaticMulticastTable. Port counters in dot1dTpPortTable cover frames for all VLANs, and 64-bit counters are added for high-capacity interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch's manual has to agree with other manuals, like the one for its network sockets. This part says how the pieces line up so nothing contradicts anything else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create can be sensitive: an insecure SET can hurt network operation. In the P-BRIDGE-MIB, tables such as dot1dPortPriorityTable and dot1dTrafficClassTable could be changed to force a reinitialization of state machines, causing instability, or to override port priority policy and give an attacker preferential treatment. In the Q-BRIDGE-MIB, objects such as dot1qVlanStaticTable and dot1qStaticUnicastTable could change VLAN operation or forwarding and filtering policy.

Read access matters too. Capability objects and tables such as dot1qVlanCurrentTable could tell an attacker which attacks might work, whether attacks are being blocked, or what the logical topology of the network looks like.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so only legitimate principals can GET or SET these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can reach the switch's dials could cause trouble or peek at how your network is laid out. So you should lock the control panel and only let trusted people in.

cells: 0 means no VLAN, 4095 means any VLAN
